title: Towards noble gas quantum optical magnetometry using direct ultraviolet detection
abstract: We analyze a novel approach for quantum magnetic sensing via optical detection of nuclear spin precession in a noble gas. The detection is carried out with an ultraviolet frequency comb laser, so no alkali vapor is required to be mixed with the noble gas during the sensing stage, allowing for hours-long spin relaxation time at room temperature. Our analysis reveals that combining high laser power and low laser intensity noise is crucial to achieving and exceeding state-of-the-art magnetometric performance, including that of cryogenic magnetometers. We find operational regimes where either fundamental or technical noise dominate, which directs experimental effort towards increasing laser power or lowering laser intensity noise, respectively. We also show that optimizing beam size is key to achieving optimal sensitivity. Our calculations predict that a record-breaking sensitivity of $24~\mathrm{aT}/\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}}$ is achievable in 10 minutes with a 10 W ultraviolet laser with a relative intensity noise of -100 dBc/Hz.
summary: This paper proposes a novel quantum optical magnetometry technique using noble gas atoms, specifically ${}^{129}	ext{Xe}$, detected via direct ultraviolet laser excitation. By eliminating the need for alkali vapors, it promises long coherence times at room temperature. Theoretical analysis predicts record-breaking magnetic field sensitivities by optimizing laser power and noise suppression techniques.
main_problem: Developing a highly sensitive and precise quantum magnetic sensing technique using noble gas atoms.
main_result: A record-breaking sensitivity of 24 aT/sqrt(Hz) is predicted, achievable with high laser power and low relative intensity noise.
method: The technique involves monitoring the oscillation of fluorescence power in ${}^{129}	ext{Xe}$ due to Larmor precession, read out using a balanced detector scheme.
model_or_system: The system uses noble gas atoms, specifically ${}^{129}	ext{Xe}$, whose nuclear spin precession is optically detected via a two-photon transition using a UV frequency comb laser. This method avoids mixing alkali vapors, allowing for long spin relaxation times at room temperature.
key_observables: Fluorescence power oscillation amplitude, Larmor frequency ($\omega_B$), and magnetic field strength ($B$).
important_parameters: High laser power (10 W), low relative intensity noise ($-100 	ext{ dBc}/	ext{Hz}$), and the spin relaxation time ($T_2$).
main_assumptions: The initial spin polarization must be created externally, and the two-photon transition is used only for reading out precession, not for pumping.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the proposed experiment schematic for Doppler-free magnetometry, and Figure 1(b) shows the energy level diagram of ${}^{129}	ext{Xe}$ detailing the two-photon transition and magnetic field interaction.
paper_structure: The paper analyzes the quantum sensing mechanism, derives the signal model based on decaying sinusoids, and performs a detailed noise analysis to determine the optimal experimental parameters for achieving maximum sensitivity.
why_interesting: This work directly applies quantum optics and atomic physics principles to build a next-generation sensor, providing quantitative predictions for performance limits based on fundamental noise sources like laser intensity noise.

FIG. 2. An example of beam size optimization, where Rf = −100 dBc/Hz, Pe = 10 W, and Tm = 10 min. The dashed lines show dependence on beam size of the sensitivity due to projection noise (orange), shot noise (green), detector noise (red), and RIN (purple). The blue solid line shows how the total sensitivity changes as a function of the beam waist, ex- hibiting a clear minimum. The corresponding optimal beam size is indicated with the black solid line.

FIG. 3. Contour plots showing each type of noise contribution to the sensitivity. In all plots the color map has the same range with the order of magnitude levels marked in black for increased clarity. a) Sensitivity due to fundamental noise, i.e., shot and projection noise. b) Sensitivity due to laser technical RIN. c) Sensitivity due to detector noise.
